item.title: What we talk about when we talk about guns: four decades of firearms coverage in the New York Times
item.dc:creator: Brett C Burkhardt; Aimee Dinnín Huff
item.description: Abstract Guns are potent cultural objects in the United States, a fact that has spurred much recent social science research. Much of that work examines the beliefs, discourses, and actions of gun enthusiasts. Less understood are the cultural dimensions of guns in the wider population, where gun owners are in the minority. This paper considers the cultural life of guns by studying the language used to depict them in a prominent US mass media outlet over four decades. We use structural topic modeling to describe the New York Times’ coverage of guns from 1980 to 2019. The analysis reveals that the coverage centers danger and societal responses to it, albeit in different ways over time. Whereas local street violence and criminal punishment dominated coverage during much of the time period, high-profile mass shootings and efforts at federal legislation have become more salient in recent years. In examining depictions of guns in mass media, the paper contributes to a growing body of literature on the cultural life of guns in US society.

item.title: Beyond hiring: the dynamics of ethnic disparities in unemployment
item.dc:creator: Raffaele Grotti; Siddartha Aradhya; Juho Härkönen
item.description: Abstract Many ethnic and racial minorities experience higher unemployment rates than majority populations. Recent research in this area has largely focused on inequalities in getting a job—through employer discrimination in hiring—using field experiments. While these studies typically identify significant levels of discrimination, they rarely examine or discuss how hiring discrimination contributes to ethnic employment penalties at the aggregate level. Our study draws attention to the role of ethnic and racial inequalities in getting a job but also in remaining employed and avoiding unemployment as factors contributing to aggregate ethnic employment penalties. Our analysis employs population register data from Sweden to estimate unemployment entry and exit rates for the majority and ten groups of children of immigrants (the second generation, G2). Based on counterfactual scenarios we conclude that the substantially higher unemployment rates among the G2 are driven by their higher risk of becoming unemployed rather than their lower chances of becoming employed. Our findings indicate that hiring discrimination and other reasons for inequalities in getting a job play a less significant role than sometimes assumed in explaining ethnic employment penalties—at least in the context of Sweden.

item.title: The triple burden: low-SES women and the binds of caretaking, work, and college
item.dc:creator: Kaylee T Matheny; Ilana M Horwitz; Natalie Milan
item.description: Abstract Scholars have identified women’s simultaneous labor force and domestic responsibilities as a “double burden” but have not fully explored how these demands intersect with pursuing higher education. Research consistently shows women’s increasing participation in higher education, with women—especially from low socioeconomic status (SES) backgrounds—outpacing men in bachelor’s degree attainment. Using nationally representative longitudinal surveys and matched educational outcome data, we examine students’ educational trajectories from their early teens through late twenties. Our findings reveal that despite gains in college enrollment and completion, low-SES women experience significantly more interruptions in their educational pursuits after enrolling in college than both low-SES men and high-SES women. Using longitudinal interviews with a matched subsample of 132 participants, we identify the presence of a “triple burden”: the simultaneous expectations of caretaking, work, and college for low-SES women. This concept contributes to the sociologies of gender, social class, domestic labor, and higher education, emphasizing the need for an intersectional understanding of the life course.

item.title: Do updates of group-level and individual-level information of ethnic minority applicants mitigate statistical discrimination in hiring?
item.dc:creator: Akira Igarashi; Susumu Cato
item.description: Abstract Labor market discrimination against ethnic minority applicants remains persistent despite extensive research and policy interventions. While social scientists have thoroughly examined statistical discrimination—wherein employers rely on group-level information to infer candidates’ future productivity due to limited individual information in resumes—fundamental questions remain unanswered regarding the relative impact of different information types. Specifically, it remains unclear whether employers are more responsive to group-level or individual–level information updates in their hiring decisions. Through a two–stage survey experiment with hiring human resources (HR) professionals at Japanese companies, this study examines how updating different types of information affects hiring discrimination. The experiment randomly updated group-level information about ethnic minority workers’ productivity (specifically, that ethnic majority and minority workers are equally productive) and provided additional individual–level applicant information. Results demonstrate that while additional individual-level information completely eliminates ethnic discrimination, updating group-level information fails to reduce discriminatory practices. Moreover, group-level information updates actually nullify the positive effects of individual-level information. These findings suggest that HR professionals’ initially low expectations of minority applicants can be easily overcome through additional individual information. However, group-level information updates raise baseline expectations and the same individual-level information becomes insufficient to exceed these elevated thresholds.

item.title: The development of inequality during primary education: investigating the genetic and environmental sources underlying learning differences
item.dc:creator: Kim Stienstra
item.description: Abstract Are differences in educational performance between pupils at the start of schooling—and their underlying genetic and environmental sources—reproduced, accumulated, or compensated over the primary school career? I investigate this using reading comprehension and mathematics test scores of over 4,000 same-sex and opposite-sex twin pairs, identified in the Netherlands Cohort Study on Education (Grades 1–5). Biometric latent growth models show, first, that most of the achievement inequality is already present at the start of education and is related to genetic variance. Second, these initial achievement differences are somewhat compensated over time, more strongly for mathematics than for reading. This leveling is related to decreasing genetic and environmental differences. Third, at the same time, new sources of achievement differences emerge during primary education that are unrelated to initial achievement. These new sources of differences are captured by variance in growth rates and are mostly genetic. As a result, although inequality linked to initial achievement decreases, the total systematic inequality in achievement increases over time because these new sources of differences outweigh the compensation of initial differences. In other words, over the course of primary education, inequality based on where children start remains prominent yet gradually decreases, while “new” inequality based on how fast children learn is simultaneously opens up.

item.title: The nonlinear nature of labor market sorting: explaining wage inequalities between and within sociodemographic groups
item.dc:creator: Lucas Sage
item.description: Abstract Sociodemographic groups with higher average wages also exhibit higher internal wage dispersion, partly explaining the overrepresentation of older, educated men in top wage percentiles. Despite being widely documented, the origins of this relationship remain poorly understood. This article proposes an explanation rooted in sorting—the tendency for workers who already command higher wages to end up in the organizations and occupations that pay the most. I argue that sorting is not merely positive but also nonlinear: its strength intensifies at higher wage levels. Because higher-wage groups experience stronger sorting, their internal wage dispersion is inflated, which contributes to the relationship between group mean wages and internal dispersion. Using French administrative data, I employ variance decompositions and simulations to quantify these effects. I find that nonlinear sorting accounts for 13% of the covariance between micro-group mean wages and internal dispersion, and for 25% of the variance in wage dispersion across groups. Simulations combined with variance function regression identify education and age as the primary dimensions along which nonlinear sorting operates. In addition, the study confirms and extends prior findings on positive sorting, showing that it accounts for 38% of between-group inequality.

item.title: One overworking breadwinner or two earners? Family economic standard of living by breadwinner arrangement, 1960 to 2018–2022
item.dc:creator: Andrew Taeho Kim
item.description: Abstract Has the rise of rewards to long and inflexible work schedules altered the household-level economic viability of gendered divisions of paid work within marriage? This paper examines whether household arrangements centered on an overworking single breadwinner have become increasingly competitive, in terms of family economic standard of living, with non-overworking dual-breadwinner households. As prior research documents increasing rewards to overwork, particularly in professional and managerial occupations, overworking single-breadwinner families may have become economically competitive with dual-breadwinner households in which neither partner overworks. Using decennial Census and American Community Survey data from the Integrated Public Use Microdata Series covering 1960 to 2018–2022, we compare breadwinner arrangements across the income distribution and decompose changes in family income into changes in men’s earnings, women’s earnings, and non-labor income. Results show that overworking male- and female-breadwinner families experienced substantial relative gains at the top of the income distribution. Decomposition analyses indicate that these gains were driven primarily by accelerated earnings growth among overworking single breadwinners rather than earnings stagnation among dual earners. Although dual-breadwinner families with overworking breadwinners remain the most advantaged group, the gap between them and overworking single-breadwinner families narrowed substantially by 2018–2022. These findings suggest that labor market reward structures associated with long and inflexible work schedules may reshape family-level economic incentives in ways that reinforce gendered divisions of paid work, particularly among affluent families.

item.title: A work of discernment: the co-construction of environmental expertise among agroecology farmers
item.dc:creator: Agueda Ortega
item.description: Abstract Agroecology—a food production and consumption model that integrates ecological, social, and economic sustainability principles—underwent a period of significant growth in recent years in Argentina. Acquiring specialized knowledge about agroecology practices is a priority for farmers who pursue socio-environmental goals, but the process for building such expertise is not clearly laid out. While some consensus exists among agroecology practitioners about key guiding principles, institutionalized knowledge about agroecology is often insufficient, inadequate, and/or contested. Further, due to a long-standing history of state support for agribusiness—a model in many ways antithetical to agroecology—agroecology practitioners are wary of institutional knowledge that may not align with their socio-environmental principles. This raises the central question of this paper: how do farmers interact with institutions to generate agroecology expertise while navigating alignments between institutional knowledge and agribusiness? Based on ethnographic observations and in-depth interviews with agroecology farmers, state workers, activists, and technicians in an agricultural town in Córdoba, Argentina, this paper examines how agroecology expertise is built among farmers. The article argues by way of empirical demonstration that expertise surges through what I term a work of discernment— a dynamic process involving the evaluation and selective combination of institutional and occupational knowledge, based on perceived alignment of priorities and goals. The paper draws from literature on expertise construction and dissemination and theorizes work of discernment as a strategy employed by non-institutional actors to generate specialized knowledge.

item.title: For what benefit? State Right to Work laws and employer-provided retirement and health insurance benefits
item.dc:creator: Alec P Rhodes
item.description: Abstract Employer-provided benefits add to total compensation and enhance economic security. Yet an increasing share of American workers lack access to employer-provided retirement and health insurance benefits, a trend that scholars link to labor union decline. I test whether state Right to Work (RTW) laws, which weaken associational worker power by targeting union security agreements, are associated with changes in employer-provided benefit coverage. Building on organizational inequality perspectives, I theorize a novel indirect impact whereby RTW conditions the returns to market-based structural worker power. I use two-way fixed effects models that leverage variation in the timing of RTW laws to estimate effects on employer-provided retirement and health insurance, relative to a control group of workers living in states that almost implemented RTW. Using pooled cross-sectional data from the 2001 to 2019 Current Population Surveys, I find that RTW weakened the inverse associations between state unemployment and retirement and health insurance benefits. Counterfactual analyses suggest declines in benefit coverage would have been lower or reversed had Indiana not implemented RTW. The findings suggest that attention to wages alone underestimate the consequences of RTW and highlight how different forms of worker power interact to shape compensation.

item.title: Fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity
item.dc:creator: Michael Grätz; Alicia García-Sierra
item.description: Abstract Different conceptions of inequality of opportunity have been developed in political philosophy. We focus on two competing conceptions: fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity. We develop an empirical framework to measure and compare these conceptions. Both fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity consider it unjust if ascribed characteristics such as social origin, gender, race, and ethnicity affect life outcomes. However, they differ in what they regard as just: fair inequality of opportunity considers it just if abilities and individual choices affect life outcomes, while luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity considers it just only if individual choices affect life outcomes. We measure fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity in education, occupation, income, and wealth using survey data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth (NLSY). Our results show that conclusions about inequality of opportunity depend on the conception of inequality of opportunity employed. From the perspective of fair inequality of opportunity, the United States is a rather just society, while the nation’s degree of luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity is high. The difference between fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity is largest for education, followed by occupation, and finally income and wealth. There is no evidence that changes across cohorts differed between fair and luck egalitarian inequality of opportunity.

item.title: Integrating or segregating? Gentrification, the changing city-suburb divide, and black exceptionalism
item.dc:creator: Jackelyn Hwang; Elizabeth Roberto; Francine I Stephens; Jacob S Rugh
item.description: Abstract Racial residential segregation has been pivotal in maintaining racial inequality following the Civil Rights Era. The transformation of cities by the spread of gentrification in recent decades may have mitigated these longstanding divisions or reproduced them as gentrification reorganizes residential patterns across urban space. However, the extent and nature of this relationship remain in question. We bridge theories of racial capitalism and residential sorting to test the racialized nature of gentrification’s prevalence, and we use a decomposition approach for measuring segregation to examine the relationship between the prevalence of gentrification and changes in segregation between various race-income groups from 1990 to 2019 across US metropolitan areas. We find that the prevalence of gentrification within central cities is associated with decreasing segregation between several groups—including poor Black and nonpoor White households—but also increasing segregation between poor minority and nonpoor White households in the suburbs and between nonpoor Black and White households overall. Altogether, the results highlight the changing spatial structure of segregation and the evolution of residential attainment for nonpoor Black households in the twenty-first century. They suggest that the spread of gentrification may contribute to dismantling longstanding patterns of segregation by race and class but may simultaneously contribute to new patterns of segregation in the suburbs and reinforce Black-White divisions.

item.title: Higher education expansion and attainment gaps in meritocratic beliefs
item.dc:creator: Angran Li; Minghao Tang
item.description: Abstract Over the past decades, higher education has expanded dramatically worldwide, yet how this transformation shapes public beliefs in meritocracy remains underexplored. This study examines how the expansion of higher education has shaped public beliefs in meritocracy across thirty Western countries. Drawing on four waves of repeated cross-national data from the International Social Survey Programme (1987, 1992, 2009, 2019, and ISSP), three-level mixed-effects models show that the gross tertiary enrollment ratio is positively associated with overall endorsement of meritocratic beliefs. Individuals with a college degree express stronger meritocratic beliefs than non-degree holders. Furthermore, the magnitude of the attainment gap increases with gross tertiary enrollment ratios, indicating that higher education expansion (HEE) reinforces belief divides. The findings suggest that HEE diffuses meritocratic norms while simultaneously stratifying their credibility across social groups. It further reveals that mass higher education generates a dual consciousness of meritocracy, combining endorsement and skepticism among individuals. The study highlights how expanding education systems shape the ideological foundations of inequality and underscores the paradoxical role of higher education as both a universalistic script and a positional resource.

item.title: Later life social interactions in community spaces
item.dc:creator: Maleah Fekete; Tianyao Qu; Brea L Perry; Siyun Peng; Adam R Roth
item.description: Abstract Daily social interactions provide access to key social resources, yet little research has examined how these interactions vary across geographic space—particularly in later life. Using ecological momentary assessment data from a state-representative study of older adults in Indiana, we examine how interactions with different partners vary across a continuum of municipality population density. Further, we assess whether this variation is shaped by social opportunity structures—such as number of community parks, theaters, and volunteer organizations—and whether patterns persist during leisure time, when individuals are free to choose their interaction partners. Results show that higher population density is associated with more time spent alone, more interactions with “shared-foci partners” (i.e., partners known through foci of activity, such as neighbors, professionals, congregation members—though associations are driven primarily by professionals, strangers, and “others”), and fewer interactions with kin. Adjusting for social opportunity structures does not affect the observed association between population density and aloneness, interactions with shared-foci partners, or interactions with kin, indicating that differential access to social opportunity spaces does not explain these relationships. Restricting analyses to leisure activities reveals that differences in shared-foci partner interactions by population density disappear—implying they are driven by variation in obligatory tasks—while differences in kin interactions and, to a lesser extent, time spent alone persist. By identifying population density as a structural factor that shapes everyday sociality, this study underscores the role of geographic context in structuring older adults’ access to social connection and the resources embedded in daily interaction.

item.title: Racism and parent stress in the context of police violence
item.dc:creator: Ann Meier; Claire Kamp Dush; Alexandra VanBergen; Sierra Clark; Hyunjae Kwon; Chalandra Bryant
item.description: Abstract This project assessed parental stress in 2020 and 2021 during a period of racial trauma marked by high-profile, race-motivated murders of people of color. We leveraged the Contextual Model of Family Stress Re-Imaged to understand parents’ stress about children’s interactions with police in the context of racism. Findings indicate higher policing stress among Black parents. To measure racism, we assessed county-level racial segregation and socioeconomic privilege, respondents’ perceptions of community climate, discrimination experiences, and the salience of George Floyd’s murder and its aftermath in their lives. The associations between Black race and discrimination experiences on the one hand and parent policing stress on the other were both direct and indirect. Black respondents and those who experienced more discrimination found more salience in the racialized milieu after George Floyd’s murder, and this was directly associated with more parent policing stress. Other indicators of racism were associated with parent policing stress indirectly. Those living in more socioeconomically privileged contexts reported a more favorable community climate, and this was associated with less policing stress. item.title: Context disadvantage and residential mobility from early life into adulthood: impacts on socio-economic outcomes
item.dc:creator: Sergi Vidal; Maël Lecoursonnais; Riccardo Valente; Maria Brandén
item.description: Abstract Individuals’ socio-economic trajectories are shaped by both persistence and change in their residential environments, making it essential to examine how the socio-spatial dynamics of context disadvantage and residential mobility interact over the life course. While prior research has often studied these factors separately and within specific life stages, less is known about their compound effects and their interrelatedness across childhood and adulthood. This study addresses this gap by investigating how exposure to residential contexts and residential mobility from birth influences socio-economic outcomes in early adulthood. Using Swedish longitudinal register data, we analyze residential trajectories and their association with economic and occupational (dis) advantage among individuals born between 1990 and 1993. Our findings show that mobility magnifies the associations between context exposure and socio-economic outcomes. Prolonged exposure to disadvantaged areas is most harmful when it coincides with moving, consistent with a compound penalty of instability and resource-poor environments. Second, moves in childhood are generally detrimental, while adult moves are opportunity-enhancing unless they occur in disadvantaged contexts, where the mobility premium levels off. Third, exiting disadvantaged contexts is associated with higher attainment than remaining persistently exposed, indicating that later socio-spatial trajectories can attenuate earlier disadvantage. These findings underscore the importance of considering both residential context and mobility across the life course for understanding—and interrupting—the reproduction of socio-economic inequality.

item.title: The stalled gender housework revolution in the United States
item.dc:creator: Patrick Ishizuka
item.description: Abstract Prior studies document a declining but persistent gender housework gap since the 1960s, with declines in women’s housework time far exceeding increases in men’s. Yet scholars differ in their assessment of what these trends mean about the pace and extent of gendered change in family life. Using individual-level longitudinal data from the 1976–2023 waves of the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, this study addresses this theoretical impasse by asking whether housework has become fundamentally degendered over time. I assess degendering using two novel indicators: the residual gender housework gap relative to the total gap and gender symmetry in associations between key predictors and housework. Results show that although the overall gender housework gap has declined substantially, the share of the total gap accounted for by theoretically relevant observed predictors remains small and has not increased over time. Individual fixed-effects models further show that cohabitation, marriage, and children remain much more strongly associated with increases in women’s housework than men’s across periods. Associations of paid work hours and earnings with housework, in contrast, attenuate over time, with less consistent evidence of gender asymmetry. Overall, these findings indicate limited progress in degendering housework and are more consistent with a stalled gender housework revolution.

item.title: Defended neighborhoods, vulnerable routines: routine activities, collective efficacy, and the social ecology of discrimination
item.dc:creator: Nicolo P Pinchak; Christopher R Browning; Bethany Boettner; J Brandon Carter; Catherine A Calder
item.description: Abstract We describe hypotheses about how features of urban settings—including location types, sociodemographic composition, and the extent of collective efficacy (CE)—are differentially related to Black and White individuals’ risks of experiencing discrimination while conducting routine activities. These hypotheses are then tested with data from a large, representative sample of caregivers in the Adolescent Health and Development in Context study (2014–2016). We find that Black individuals are twice as likely as White individuals to report experiencing discrimination in their routine activities, and this Black-White gap is further increased among workplaces, grocery stores, and businesses relative to other locations. Additionally, Black and White individuals report similarly increased probabilities of experiencing discrimination at schools. Consistent with an extension of research on “defended neighborhoods,” exposure to higher CE is positively associated with discrimination for Black individuals especially among areas high in socioeconomic status or high in proportion White population. However, for White individuals, exposure to higher CE is negatively associated with discrimination especially among areas low in socioeconomic status or low in proportion White population. This study underscores that measuring social processes at routine activity settings, rather than just in home neighborhoods, is essential for research on everyday well-being. Further, the findings complement calls to invest in the resource capacity of high-poverty and low-proportion White neighborhoods.

item.title: Whose merit, which redistribution? Elites, taxes, and transfers in Brazil and South Africa
item.dc:creator: Livio Silva-Muller; Graziella Moraes Silva; Matias López
item.description: Abstract Scholarship often treats two dimensions of meritocracy as interchangeable: if success is due to hard work, poverty must be due to a lack of effort. We contrast elites’ perceptions about their own success with their perceptions about the lack of success of others. We posit that these two dimensions—merit of self and merit of others—are distinct, with different implications for redistributive preferences, and varying salience across national contexts. Using data from elite surveys in Brazil and South Africa, we examine whose merit matters for giving income to policies (transfers) versus taking income from policies (taxation). We show that elites are more likely to credit their own success to hard work than to attribute poverty to lack of effort, and that these two dimensions are independent. Perceiving the poor as effortless, rather than elites as hard-working, predict opposition to transfers. In contrast, elites' perceptions of self play a context-dependent role. In Brazil, they are associated with opposition to taxation but are confounded with political identification, while in South Africa, redistributive preferences are structured primarily by racial identification. We interpret these cross-national differences considering distinct trajectories of state-building and inequality.

item.title: Having a child through medically assisted reproduction: a social stratification perspective
item.dc:creator: Alice Goisis; Alina Pelikh; Maria Palma; Pekka Martikainen; Niina Metsä-Simola; Hanna Remes
item.description: Abstract Prior research documents marked social disparities in births through medically assisted reproduction (MAR), which are often attributed to unequal access to treatment. However, social inequalities may also arise from processes operating after MAR treatments begin. We examine this possibility using population-level administrative register data from Finland, a context where MAR treatments are generously subsidized and access barriers are relatively low. Focusing on all childless women who initiated MAR treatments between 1995 and 2019, we analyze whether and why women with tertiary education are more likely than less-educated women to have a child through MAR. The results show that, among childless women who start MAR treatments, those with tertiary education are more likely to have a child after MAR than women with below tertiary education. This educational gradient is partly explained by differences in early treatment discontinuation, uptake of more invasive and more successful MAR treatments, and per-cycle treatment success rates. The results support the hypothesis that social stratification processes in MAR outcomes continues after the start of MAR treatments.

item.title: Bad timing: mass-participatory asset bubbles as a mechanism of predatory inclusion
item.dc:creator: Adam Goldstein; Max Fineman
item.description: Abstract This paper considers the relationship between market composition and temporal dynamics of ethno-racial stratification in mass-participatory asset bubbles. Beginning from the insight that bubbles possess the social structure of a Ponzi scheme, we first ask to what extent timing of entry is structured by racial status and associated resource disparities among participants. We then consider to what extent homophilous social cues and segregation amplify disparate rates of late-stage entry. We focus on the 2000–2008 US residential housing market, using neighborhood-level data from the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act and the Federal Housing Finance Authority. Conditional on mortgage lending terms, credit availability, and other tract-level characteristics, trends in housing purchase rates for Blacks and Hispanics diverged from those of Whites as prices neared their peaks. Residential segregation and processes of homophilous diffusion amplify price-bidding and exacerbate racial disparities in rates of late-stage entry by rendering actors less attuned to the emergent risks of buying at elevated prices, and more vulnerable to the overtures of predatory agents. The analysis links the sociology of financial markets to studies of racialized predatory inclusion by considering heterogenous market timing, a mechanism which has become increasingly salient as financialization draws more diverse actors into volatile asset markets.

item.title: The code of cohesion: adolescent network centrality, offending, and the downside of school cohesion
item.dc:creator: Nicolo P Pinchak
item.description: Abstract Paradoxical to numerous theories and policies, adolescents attending schools high in student cohesion do not reliably exhibit less involvement in offending. Coleman’s arguments about status and norms and the broader literature on adolescent networks suggest that this paradox is partially attributable to high-status males having more leeway to offend when attending schools high in student cohesion, which over time reinforces their engagement in offending. Here, an initial test of this “code of cohesion” hypothesis is conducted using data from high school students in Waves I–III of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health. Adolescents’ status positions at school are identified using multiple measures of network centrality, and high-cohesion schools are identified as those high on measures of student friendship network density or school social climate. Consistent with the hypothesis, results indicate that the positive association of male adolescents’ network centrality with offending becomes increasingly evident over time when they attend high-cohesion schools and diminishes over time after exiting these schools. Among schools of low/moderate-cohesion, the association of males’ network centrality with offending is less evident and does not persist after exiting schooling whatsoever. These findings support Coleman’s arguments about status and norms enabling leeway and illuminate a key reason why efforts to reduce offending by fostering student cohesion have had limited success. Additionally, this study highlights the need for research assessing how school relational dynamics among teachers, administrators, and parents, in addition to adolescent social systems, shape adolescents’ behavioral trajectories.

item.title: Multiracial young adults’ experiences of Whiteness as a wage and tax
item.dc:creator: Monica Heilman
item.description: Abstract Debates persist on the racial position of multiracial Americans, namely whether this population will “become White” or not. However, the premise of this question is predicated on a monoracial paradigm of race that cannot fully account for the experiences of multiracial individuals. Multiracial experiences with Whiteness, including ways they conform to and confound monoracial expectations, have the potential to reshape our understandings of racial constructions, boundaries, and futures, particularly considering shifting racial demographics. One necessary precursor toward these insights lies in the distinctions between how multiracial and monoracial individuals experience Whiteness. Drawing on thirty-seven in-depth interviews with multiracial young adults with White ancestry in the Midwest, I argue that multiracial individuals experience Whiteness as a wage (privileges) and a tax (costs). Like monoracial Whites, multiracial individuals viewed as White can receive public and psychological wages, yet these wages are offset by an inseparable “racial tax,” which is predicated on the contingent and exclusive nature of Whiteness. These results underscore the utility of calling attention to the monoracial structure, as well as recognizing and theorizing beyond its limits.

item.title: Festivalized marriage as a Time Threshold: Spring Festival bottlenecks, Qualification Audits, and escalating entry standards in rural China
item.dc:creator: Yong Yu; Keke Qin; Wenzhao Huang; Shishi Tang
item.description: Abstract When do institutional calendars become stratifying devices rather than neutral schedules of action? Drawing on two Spring Festival windows in villages under Yingchunting Subdistrict, Wugang, Hunan, this article shows that rural bachelors’ marriage seeking becomes festivalized: compressed into a recurrent return window where families, matchmakers, and prospective spouses assemble evidence, compare candidates, and clear outcomes before migrants disperse. We theorize Spring Festival as a Time Threshold: a window-deadline-clearing structure that synchronizes dispersed actors and converts courtship into concentrated evaluation. Inside this threshold, a Qualification Audit makes hypergamy auditable by translating marriageability and county-seat mobility into evidence bundles of housing, renovation progress, cash flow, bridewealth timing, parental backstops, reputation, and interactional fit. The window also creates Outcome Filing and Threshold Escalation: advancement, suspension, ghosting, and failure travel as records that alter next-cycle starting positions and evidentiary demands. Combining 114 interviews with 94 participants, 224 hours of observation, 41 reconstructed chains, and 297 de-identified artifacts, the article specifies when calendars stratify: recurrent deadlines, synchronized availability, high-stakes qualification, portable evidence, and outcomes that travel. The mechanism speaks beyond rural China to admissions cycles, visa windows, hiring seasons, and other institutional calendars that convert unequal life chances into auditable records with cumulative consequences.

item.title: Explaining gendered language through embedding approximation: how “stupid” became a man’s word
item.dc:creator: Yutong Zhu
item.description: Abstract Recent advances in word embedding have reinvigorated macro-historical cultural analysis based on empirical data. However, these methods primarily model the semantic structure of language, which can obscure the pragmatic dimension of language use central to sociology. Focusing on a previous study of “unintelligence” words in 20th-century American discourse, I investigate the puzzling finding that these words became more male-aligned over time. I argue there is a one-to-many mapping between low-level distance in the embedding space and high-level cultural meanings, and reconsider the stereotype-based interpretation of the changing gender alignment of “unintelligence” words. While the gender axis reliably measures gendered associations, distance-based associations do not neatly map onto well-defined gender stereotypes. Cross-validating embedding alignments against direct co-occurrence with gender-identity words, I first demonstrate that the masculinization of “unintelligence” is unlikely to be driven by judgments directed at gendered persons. Applying an adapted A La Carte (ALC) approximation of individual context words and sentences, I then characterize the pragmatic register of the influential context words—their tone and stance—through close reading validated against the NRC Emotion Lexicon: the contexts driving masculinization shifted from affiliative ease (“soft” contexts, e.g., “adored,” “wholesome”) toward confrontational intensity (“harsh” contexts, e.g., “sin,” “shout”). Robustness checks across randomly sampled word sublists confirm that this pragmatic register shift, not changing judgments of male intellect, is associated with the masculinization. This study demonstrates the interpretive gap in embedding-based methods and calls for more rigorous approaches to intersubjectively valid interpretation of cultural change.

item.title: Filling the collective-practice gap: pedagogies of participation in participatory-democratic organizations
item.dc:creator: Amanda B Cox
item.description: Abstract Participatory-democratic organizations seek to redistribute decision-making authority, but doing so raises a practical question: how do participants learn to exercise that authority in nonhierarchical, collective ways? This paper theorizes how participatory-democratic organizations address what I term the collective-practice gap: the gap between the individualistic capacities shaped in hierarchical institutions and the relational, participatory capacities required for nonhierarchical, collective participation. Drawing on ethnographic research in two participatory-democratic organizations—a democratic school and a community-governed philanthropic project—I examine how democratic capacity is cultivated through everyday organizational practice. I identify two dilemmatic pedagogical strategies used by experienced participants: the non-exercise of influence and taking the long view. Through these relational and temporal practices, experienced members strategically withhold outcome-directing intervention and tolerate slow, inefficient, or uncertain processes, creating conditions for others to develop the skills, values, and behaviors needed to function in a democratic, collective setting. These strategies, however, carry organizational risks—including delay, conflict, and uneven participation—because the practices that support democratic learning can also strain organizational functioning. Therefore, these strategies are best understood not as fixed solutions but as partial, situational responses to the tension between cultivating egalitarian participation and preserving organizational viability.

item.dc:creator: Braulio Güémez
item.description: Abstract This paper examines the intergenerational transmission of Indigenous classification in Mexico, focusing on how respondents reproduce, reject, or adopt Indigenous identification in relation to how they classify their parents. Drawing on data from a novel, nationally representative survey, I analyze factors associated with two key trajectories: de-indigenization, in which respondents who classify at least one parent as Indigenous do not self-classify as Indigenous, and indigenization, in which individuals who claim no Indigenous parentage come to identify as Indigenous. The findings show that roughly 16 percent of the population differs from how they report their parents’ Indigenous status. Reports of the loss of Indigenous language across generations are primarily associated with de-indigenization. In contrast, perceived phenotypical features commonly linked to Indigenous belonging and reports of Indigenous language proficiency are more strongly associated with indigenization. Additionally, a notable subset (10 percent) identifies as both Indigenous and mestizo, a classification path correlated with higher levels of education. These patterns reveal the fluidity of ethnoracial boundaries in Mexico and illustrate how processes of cultural transmission, racialization, and stratification shape the social production of Indigenous identity through different pathways.

item.title: Sex differences in academic achievement in US adolescents: the role of maturation and impulse control
item.dc:creator: Liza Reisel; Atika Khurana
item.description: Abstract This study investigates mechanisms underlying girls’ academic advantage over boys by examining the role of physical and pubertal maturation. Using longitudinal data from the Add Health study, we analyzed whether sex differences in maturation explain girls’ higher grade 10 GPAs, and whether these associations are mediated by planfulness or impulse control. Path analysis revealed that females’ higher GPAs were partially explained by their advanced physical maturation as rated by the interviewer (explaining 2.4 percent) and greater impulse control (explaining 7.7 percent), controlling for cognitive ability and other potential confounders. Still, a significant direct effect of biological sex on GPA remained, suggesting additional unexplained mechanisms. Planfulness predicted GPA but did not vary by sex, and neither planfulness nor impulse control were associated with perceived relative maturation.

item.title: The magic of secularization
item.dc:creator: Paul Froese; Isaiah King; Ruiqian Li
item.description: Abstract Institutional secularization does not necessitate a secular public. In fact, as church memberships decline, more individualized sources of supernatural belief can emerge. Using a nationally representative survey of American adults (n = 1812), we analyze the popularity of “secular rationalism” and how it relates to belief in non-Divine supernatural causation, i.e., magic. Our findings suggest that belief in magic is not simply the inverse of religiosity or secular rationalism. Instead, belief in magic emerges most strongly among those who are both scientifically oriented and residually religious. Secular rationalism does not erase belief in supernatural mechanisms—it affirms the individual’s agency to decide what they are. In short, magic thrives where reason and spirituality meet, suggesting that modernity’s rational turn does not disenchant so much as release faith from institutional restraints.

item.title: University expansion, academic fields, and the match between the degree and the job
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Horowitz; Sagi Ramaj
item.description: Abstract Academic knowledge—such as biology, psychology, and economics—is found both in university majors and specific occupations. When educational attainment expands in the population, does it improve or weaken the academic match between university majors and occupations? Using nationally representative data from Great Britain and Canada, we find heterogeneous effects by field of study that are consistent across countries. Increases in the proportion of individuals with university degrees improves matches for economics, mathematics, and fine arts majors, such that they enter occupations that utilize more of their major-specific academic knowledge. The reverse is true for graduates in philosophy and theology, sociology and anthropology, and several majors in the natural and physical sciences. While some high-status fields see stronger matches between major and occupation as education expands, the natural and physical sciences remain a clear exception. These idiosyncratic results suggest that field-level prestige partly explains the heterogeneous effects of educational expansion on major-occupation matching, but that more research is needed on shifts in academic knowledge usage in the labor market.

item.title: When hazards don’t make law: structural resonance in global disaster-law diffusion, 1960–2025
item.dc:creator: Maoxin Ye; Daniel P Aldrich
item.description: Abstract This article asks why states adopt comprehensive national disaster laws. Rather than treating legislation as an automatic response to hazard exposure, we conceptualize disaster-law adoption as a process of structural resonance: regional diffusion pressures become consequential when they align with domestic governance needs and administrative capacity. Using a new country-year dataset of first adoptions across 204 states and territories from 1960 to 2025, we estimate Cox proportional hazards models with multiple imputation. Recent hazard exposure predicts adoption only in simpler specifications and loses significance once diffusion and state-structure variables are introduced. Regional adoption share strongly accelerates first adoption. Decentralization and government accountability are also associated with earlier enactment, and regional diffusion is amplified in more decentralized polities. The findings show that disaster legalization is not simply a functional response to risk. It is a sociological process in which external legal templates gain force where domestic authority is fragmented and the demand for administrative coordination is high.

item.title: Beneath consensus: political framing of gender-based violence in the Italian press, 2005–2023
item.dc:creator: Ester Fanelli
item.description: Abstract Discourse on gender-based violence started as a political struggle driven by feminist movements allied with progressive parties in the 1970s. However, in recent years, both progressive and conservative Italian parties have proposed and approved laws to combat gender-based violence. The combination of cross-partisan legislation and sharp cultural divisions makes Italy an interesting case for examining how polarization can persist alongside legislative consensus. This study draws on a large corpus of newspaper articles (7,978) from progressive, moderate, and conservative national outlets to address the following questions: How did the distribution of frames of gender-based violence vary across the political spectrum between 2005 and 2023 (ideological polarization)? Did newspapers make explicit adversarial claims against the opposing political side (affective polarization), and if so, around which frames? Combining Structural Topic Modeling and qualitative content analysis, this article shows that the salience of gender-based violence increased across the political spectrum. However, ideological polarization persists regarding how newspapers describe gender-based violence and which solutions they privilege, with progressives increasingly focusing on preventive, rather than punitive, interventions. At the same time, gender-based violence became a catalyst for deep partisan divisions around gender identity and immigration, two discursive overlaps that fuel affective polarization. By examining the framing process as a site of both ideological and affective polarization, this study bridges the literatures on social problems and political polarization and provides a data-driven understanding about the actual content of opposing positions.

item.title: Job precarity and earnings inequality in contemporary China
item.dc:creator: Zhipeng Zhou
item.description: Abstract Job precarity is a core mechanism of workplace inequality that underlies economic segmentation between organizational insiders and outsiders. Yet less is known about how institutional contexts affect dual employment arrangements that create differential rewards between long-term and short-term workers. Drawing on institutional distinctions between China’s state and private sectors under marketization, this study shows how compensation for employment relations differ across sectors, how sector-specific returns vary with marketization levels, and how these differential returns contribute to overall earnings inequality within sectors. In the private sector, labor flexibility helps offset the costs of maintaining long-term employment through lower pay for short-term workers. In the state sector, the socialist personnel system preserves advantages for permanent employees, whereas the economic egalitarianism norms constrain the sustainability of these advantages under dual employment relations. Analyzing data from the nationally representative China Family Panel Studies 2018 and leveraging provincial marketization variations, I find that the state sector has less employment precarity than the private sector overall but imposes a larger earnings penalty on short-term employment. This penalty is smaller in more marketized provinces, mitigating overall earnings inequality associated with employment type within the state sector. In the private sector, however, both forms of inequality are larger in more marketized provinces. These within-sector earnings penalties and their association with marketization are most pronounced among low-paid workers, and cross-sector disparities are concentrated between government and public institutions and private enterprises. The findings challenge the view that marketization uniformly worsens precarious workers’ earnings and demonstrate the institutional foundations of labor market inequality in contemporary China.

item.title: Paving the way: redlining and contemporary transportation emissions in US cities
item.dc:creator: Rachel McKane; Patrick Trent Greiner
item.description: Abstract We expand upon the structural human ecology tradition by recasting its classic drivers as historically racialized mechanisms operating within a system of racial capitalism. We draw on critical approaches to environmental justice to link multiscalar processes to material infrastructures, theorizing redlining and interstate-highway planning as coupled racial projects that organize the production of transportation emissions across urban space. To test this empirically, we combine Home Owners’ Loan Corporation grades with on-road carbon dioxide (CO₂) and estimate multilevel models for 9661 census tracts nested in 194 US cities (2010, 2015). Redlined areas exhibit higher on-road CO₂ net of contemporary tract characteristics. Associations between affluence, whiteness, and emissions are strong in greenlined areas but largely flat in redlined areas, and public-transit commuting shares show little relationship to emissions across grades. Together, the results indicate that spatially fixed, historically racialized transport infrastructure continues to concentrate emissions in disinvested neighborhoods regardless of who lives there now.

item.title: Framing inclusion: discursive logics of entitlement in immigrant social rights advocacy
item.dc:creator: Mara Junge
item.description: Abstract This article investigates how civil society organizations (CSOs) advocate for immigrant access to social assistance in politically charged environments. It explores whether the frame choices of CSOs are shaped by their relationships with government bodies and examines the implications of these narratives for representing a highly diverse group of non-citizens. The article introduces a novel two-dimensional framework that categorizes advocacy frames along two axes: “scope of inclusion” (Targeted Inclusion vs. Universal Inclusion) and “justification for entitlement” (Individual Justification vs. Structural Justification). Findings from document analysis reveal a predominant reliance on frames that call for the inclusion of specific groups basing entitlement on individual characteristics independent of CSOs’ relationship to the state. The most radical frame type (Structural Justification for Universal Inclusion), however, is more frequently used by independent CSOs. Analyses of interviews underscore that CSOs navigate a trade-off: aligning with targeted, individualistic frames can achieve incremental policy gains, but potentially reinforces stratified notions of “deservingness”, contributing to internal hierarchies within immigrant communities. Conversely, advancing structural justification for universal inclusion carries the potential to challenge systemic inequalities yet risks limited immediate resonance within the political mainstream. These insights highlight the tension between short-term policy success and long-term systemic change in CSO advocacy strategies. The empirical findings, alongside theoretical discussions, extend beyond this specific policy field, offering broader insights into civil society strategies in adverse contexts.

item.title: Organizational status and online-offline mobilization cycles
item.dc:creator: Jack G R Wippell
item.description: Abstract Scholars of social movements and culture are increasingly interested in the dynamic relationship between online discourse and offline mobilization. Although prior work typically frames online discourse as a precursor to offline activism, emerging research on right-wing extremist (RWE) mobilization hints at a reciprocal relationship. Recognizing the group-based organizational structure of many contemporary social movements, I put forward a framework for understanding online-offline mobilization cycles by extending status theories of collective action to organizational processes and networks. An analysis of the white supremacist movement White Lives Matter provides preliminary support for the theory, with implications for wider debates in scholarship on social movements, online discourse, and organizational processes.

item.title: Working from home among older adults in the UK: examining its link to labor market exit intentions and expected retirement age
item.dc:creator: Yanan Zhang; Sarah Harper; Senhu Wang; Bing Gong
item.description: Abstract Prolonging work life has been widely discussed in countries facing population aging. We examine the association between working from home (WFH) and both the labor market exit intentions and expected retirement age among the older workforce in the UK, utilizing data from the harmonized British Household Panel Survey (BHPS) and the UK Household Longitudinal Survey (UKHLS), covering the period from September 1998 to May 2020. Findings indicate that WFH is linked to reduced labor market exit intentions and a later expected retirement age, through improved subjective well-being. The association between WFH and expected retirement age is significantly stronger among women than among men. The estimated associations for the labor market exit intentions are also larger among women, although the corresponding gender interaction terms are not statistically significant. Additionally, the specific domains of subjective well-being that mediate the link between WFH and the labor market exit intentions differ between men and women. These insights support enhancing WFH policies to keep older adults economically active, which improves their well-being and advances gender equality by prolonging older women’s careers.

item.title: Do caring fathers earn less? Earnings consequences of fathers’ parental leave use
item.dc:creator: Corinna Frodermann; Ann-Christin Bächmann; Andreas Filser
item.description: Abstract In many Western societies, policy efforts seek to increase fathers’ involvement in parental leave, yet many fathers remain reluctant due to concerns about earnings consequences. Despite these concerns, the consequences of parental leave and their underlying mechanisms remain understudied. Using novel German administrative data on 109,735 married fathers who became first-time parents between 2007 and 2013, we analyze their earnings trajectories following parental leave. The large sample allows for investigating potential differences in earnings trajectories between fathers who took no parental leave and fathers who took leave of different durations. To improve comparability between the different groups of fathers, we apply two-way fixed-effects models weighted by coarsened exact matching. Moreover, the data enables us to consider differences in post-birth work volume as potential confounder for differences in earnings trajectories. We find that fathers who take parental leave experience lower earnings trajectories compared with those without leave. This difference increases with leave duration: 7 years after the birth of their first child, fathers who took up to 2 months of leave see their annual earnings increase 2.2 percentage points less relative to their pre-birth baseline than fathers who took no leave—for those who took longer leave, the gap is 12.8 percentage points. While these gaps initially appear disproportionately larger for longer leave durations, the disparity diminishes once we account for differences in active employment and part-time transitions. Moreover, the differences in work volume explain a large share of the observed earnings gaps, reducing them to 1 and 4.6 percentage points.
